title: Mountains and Waters
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares a Native American story called "Jumping Mouse" about a mouse who discovers new insights and perspectives through exploration and understanding, illustrating the idea that our perceptions can be expanded beyond our individual limits. The story teaches us to approach life with humility and openness, recognizing that our experiences are interconnected and that we have the power to transform ourselves and others. By embracing this perspective, we can heal and connect with one another, ultimately realizing our shared nature as "eagles" in spirit.

sentences.text: Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra, recently chanted on the trail below Mount Baker.
*Because green mountains walk, they are stable and still.
Although they walk more swiftly than the wind, someone in the mountains does not notice or understand.
In the mountains means the blossoming of the entire world.
People outside the mountains do not notice or understand the mountains walking.
Those without eyes to see mountains cannot notice, understand, or hear this.
So clearly examine the green mountains walking and your own walking.

Examine walking backward and walking forward and backward walking and forward walking, and investigate the fact that walking forward and backwards has never stopped since before the very moment form arose.*
*Because mountains are high and broad, their way of riding the clouds always extends from the mountains.
The wondrous power of soaring in the winds come freely from the mountains.
Water is neither strong nor weak, nor wet nor dry, neither moving nor still, neither cold nor hot.
Water is neither existent or non-existent, neither diluted nor enlightened.
When water solidifies, it is harder than a diamond.
Who can crack it?
When water melts, it is softer than milk.
Who could destroy it?
When dragons and fish see water as a palace, they may not realize that it flows.
They may not think it flows.
If an outsider tells them, "What you see as a palace, dear dragon or fish, is running water," the dragons and fish may be astonished, just as we are when we hear the words of mountains flow.*
*Nevertheless, there may be some dragons and fish who understand that railings and pillars of palaces and pavilions are flowing water.
Although mountains belong to the nation, but mountains belong to people who love them.
When mountains love their master, a wise person enters the mountains.
Since mountains belong to the wise people living there, trees and rocks are abundant and birds and animals are inspired.
There are mountains hidden in treasures.
There are mountains hidden in swamps.
There are mountains hidden in the sky.
There are mountains hidden in mountains.
There are mountains hidden in hiddenness.
This is how we study because mountains belong to the nation, mountains belong to people who love them.*
So beautiful, huh?
And so like, huh?
Both.
We were talking about this.
We chanted it along the trail, and then one evening after Zazen we went out in this little meadow as the sun went down and we talked about it.
Unfortunately we got so into talking about it that we got a chill to the bone.
It was really hard to get warm again that night for several of us.
It gets cold in the mountains.
But anyway, we were just trying to puzzle it out together, which was fun, a little bit like Chris's Dogen group.
One of our members, Kit, said it was really for him all about perspective and seeing things a different way, depending on where you are and how you look.
He said it reminded him of a powerful native story called the story of Jumping Mouse, which he summarized for us.
That struck a chord for me, actually, because I knew the story of Jumping Mouse and I'd forgotten it.
One of the most important parts of my education was my senior year of high school.
I transferred to a different school to participate in this tiny alternative school.
One teacher, 18 students, it was called the learning community.
This teacher was just a brilliant, wise, young guy.
He figured these kids need something integrated and they need community.
They don't need to just go to English and then to math and then blah, blah, blah.
So he integrated all these things together and somehow sold the school board on it.
I think because he just didn't cause trouble, they let him do it for 30 years.
The minute he retired, the [unclear: "burden"] was like gone.
But it was really powerful for me.
Very integrative, project-based, community-oriented, lots of community decisions, consensus decisions about our curriculum.
When does that happen in high school?
Gary Bacon is a teacher.
Gary also managed to slide in lots of spirituality and philosophy, things that high school kids in middle class America had never heard of at all.
And I was actually in that program when I had my first visit to his [unclear: "end center"].
You can see that must have stuck.
So anyhow, Gary also read us the same story.
So in honor of Gary, who I got to see last April, he's 85 or 86 now, doing pretty good, I want to share with you, too, the story of Jumping Mouse.
It's a Dharma story.
All good stories are, really.
I do always worry and wonder a little, telling a Native story, whether it's really true to the original.
When the settlers and anthropologists and whoever collected them, [unclear: "gimme"], they often cleaned them up and made them sound more like Western stories.
But this one appears to be a fairly legit Plains Indian Sundance story.
I can ask Jeff sometime if he's heard this.
It's Sundance, Jeff.
Kate's husband has been to Sundance many times.
So here's the story of Jumping Mouse.
Please be comfortable.
Enjoy the story.
Let's see what we can learn about from this little mouse.
Once there was a mouse.
He was a busy mouse, searching everywhere, touching his whiskers to the grass and looking around.
He was busy as all mice are, busy with mice things.
But once in a while, he would hear an odd sound.
He would lift his head, squinting hard to see, his whiskers wriggling in the air, and he would wonder, what is that sound?
One day he scurried to his fellow mouse and asked him, "Do you hear a roaring in your ears, my brother?"
"No, no," answered the other mouse, not lifting his busy nose from the ground.
"I hear nothing.
I am busy.
Talk to me later."
He asked another mouse the same question.
The mouse looked at him very strangely.
"Are you foolish in your head?
What sound?" he asked, and slipped into a hole in a fallen cottonwood tree.
So the mouse shrugged his whiskers and busied himself again, determined to forget the whole matter.
But there was that roaring again.
It was faint, very faint.
But there it was.
So one day he decided he really had to investigate.
Leaving the other busy mice, he scurried a little ways away and listened again.
There it was.
He was listening hard and suddenly someone else said, "Hello."
"Hello, little brother," the voice said.
And the mouse almost jumped right out of his skin.
"Oops, sorry."
He arched his back and tail and was about to run.
"Hello, again," said the voice.
"It is I, Raccoon."
And sure enough it was.
"What are you doing here all by yourself, little brother?" asked Raccoon.
And the mouse blushed and put his nose to the ground and said a little bit timidly, "I hear a roaring in my ears.
I'm investigating."
"A roaring in your ears," replied Raccoon as he sat down with him.
"What you hear, little brother, is the river."
"The river?" the mouse asked curiously.
"What is a river?"
"Walk with me and I'll show you the river," Raccoon said.
Little Mouse was terribly afraid, but he was determined to find out once and for all about this roaring.
"I can return to my work," he thought, "after this thing is settled.
And possibly this thing may aid me in all my busy examining and collecting.
And my brother said it was nothing.
I will show them.
I will ask Raccoon to return with me and I will have proof."
"All right, Raccoon, my brother," said the mouse, "lead on to the river.
I will walk with you."
So Little Mouse walked with Raccoon, his little heart pounding in his breast.
Raccoon was walking him along some strange paths and Little Mouse *smelled the scent of many things that had gone by this way.
Many times he became so frightened he almost turned back.
Finally they came to the river.
It was huge and breathtaking, deep and clear in places and murky in others.
Little mouse was unable to see across.
It was so great.
It roared, sang, cried and thundered on its course.* [unclear: "What little mouse saw"] *great and little pieces of the world carried along on its surface.
"It is powerful," little mouse said, fumbling for words.
"It is a great thing," answered raccoon.
"But here, let me introduce you to a friend."*
*In a smoother, shallower place was a lily pad, bright and green.
Sitting upon it was a frog, almost as green as the pad it sat on.
The frog's white belly stood out clearly.
"Hello, little brother," said the frog.
"Welcome to the river."
"I'll leave it to you now," [unclear: "cut in"] raccoon.
"But do not fear, little brother.
Frog will take care of you now."
And raccoon left, looking along the riverbank for food that he might wash and eat.*
*Little mouse approached the river and looked into it.
He saw a frightened mouse reflected there.
"Who are you?" little mouse asked the reflection.
"Are you not afraid of being far out in that great river?"
"No," answered frog for his reflection.
"I'm not afraid.
I've been given the gift from birth to live both above and within the river.
When winter man comes and freezes this medicine, I cannot be seen.
But while thunderbird flies, I am here.
To visit me, one must come when the world is green.
I, my brother, am the keeper of the water."*
*"Amazing," little mouse said, again fumbling for words.
"Would you like to have some medicine power?" frog asked.
"Medicine power?
Me?" asked little mouse.
"Yes, yes, if it's possible."
"Ah, then crouch as low as you can and jump as high as you are able.
You will have your medicine," frog said.
Little mouse did as he was instructed.
Crouched as low as he could and jumped.
When he did, his eyes saw beyond the river, the sacred mountains.
Little mouse could hardly believe his eyes, but there they were.
Then he fell back to earth and he landed in the river.*
*Little mouse became very frightened and scrambled back to the bank.
He was wet and frightened nearly to death.
"You tricked me!" little mouse screamed at the frog.
"Wait," said frog.
"You're not harmed?
Do not let your anger and fear blind you.
What did you see?"
"I," mouse stammered, "I saw the sacred mountains."
"Ah, and you have a new name too," said frog.
"It is jumping mouse."
"Thank you, thank you," jumping mouse said, and thanked him again.
"I must return to my people and tell them about this thing that has happened to me."
"Go, go then," frog said.
"Return to your people.
It's easy to find them.
Keep the sound of the medicine river to the back of your head.
Go opposite the sound.
You'll find your brother mice."*
*So jumping mouse returned to the world of the mice.
You can imagine what happens next.
He found disappointment.
No one would listen to him.
And because he was wet and had no way of explaining this, because there had been no rain, many of the other mice were frightened of him.
They believed he had been spat from the mouth of an animal that had tried to eat him.
And they all knew that if he had not been food for the one who wanted him, he must be poison.*
*So jumping mouse tried to live among his people, but he could not forget this vision of the sacred mountains and he could not forget the river.
The memory burned in his mind and burned in the mind and heart of jumping mouse.
And one day he went to the edge of the place of mice and looked again out into the prairie.
He looked up for eagles.
The sky was full of many spots, each one an eagle.
But he was determined to go to the sacred mountains if he could.
He gathered all his courage and ran just as fast as he could onto the prairie, his little heart pounding with excitement and fear.*
*He ran until he came to a stand of sage, like sagebrush.
He was resting and trying to catch his breath and he saw an old mouse.
The patch of sage old mouse lived in was a haven for mice.
Seeds and many things he was busy with.
"Hello," said old mouse, "welcome."
Jumping mouse was amazed.
Such a place, such a mouse.
"You must be a truly great mouse," jumping mouse said with respect.
"This is a truly wonderful place, and the eagles cannot see you here either."*
*"Yes," said old mouse, "and one can see all the beings of the prairie here, the buffalo, antelope, rabbit and coyote.
One can see them all and know their names."
"That is marvelous," jumping mouse said.
"Can you also see the river and the great mountains?"
"Yes and no," the old mouse said with conviction.
"I know the great river but I am afraid that the mountains are only a myth.
Forget your passion for them and stay here with me.
There is everything you want to see.
It is a good place to be."
"How can you say such a thing," [unclear: "like jumping mouse"]?
"The medicine of the sacred mountains is nothing one can forget.
Thank you for the meal that you shared with me, old mouse, and also for sharing your great home," jumping mouse said, "but I must seek the mountains."*
*"You are a foolish mouse to leave.
There is danger on the prairie.
Just look up there," the old mouse said with even more conviction.
"See all those spots?
They are eagles.
They will catch you."
It was hard for jumping mouse to leave but he gathered his determination and ran hard.
The ground was rough.
He arched his tail and ran with all his might.
He could feel the shadows of the spots on his back as he ran.
All those white spots.*
*Finally he ran into a stand of choked cherries.
Jumping mouse could hardly believe his eyes.
It was cool there and very spacious.
There was water, cherries and seeds to eat, grasses to gather for nests, holes to be explored and many other busy things to do.
There were a great many things to gather.
He was investigating his new domain and he heard very heavy breathing.
He quickly investigated the sound and discovered its source.
It was a great mound of hair with black horns.
It was a great buffalo.*
*Jumping mouse could hardly believe the greatness of the being he saw lying there before him.
It was so large that jumping mouse could have crawled into one of his great horns.
"Such a magnificent being," thought jumping mouse, and he crept closer.*
I'm sorry, this piece didn't make it here, so we can go to this other page.
Okay.
*"Hello, my brother, hello, my brother," said the buffalo.
"You're right.
Thank you for visiting me."
"Hello, [unclear: "great beings of"] jumping mouse.
Why are you lying there?"
"I am sick and I am dying,*
*buffalo said.
"And my medicine has told me that only the eye of a mouse can heal me.
But little brother, there's no such thing as a mouse."
Jumping mouse was shocked.
"One of my eyes," he thought?
"One of my tiny eyes?"
He scurried back into the stand of choked cherries, but the breathing came harder and slower.
Jumping mouse was moved.
"He will die if I do not give him my eye, and he is too great of a being to let die."
So he went back to where buffalo lay and he spoke.
"I am a mouse, I am a mouse," he said with a shaky voice.
"And you, my brother, a great being, I cannot let you die.
I have two eyes.
You may have one of them."
The minute he said it, jumping mouse's eye flew out of his head and the buffalo was made whole.
The buffalo jumped to his feet, shaking and jumping, jumping and shaking little mouse's whole world.*
*"Thank you, little brother," said the buffalo.
"I know of your great quest for the sacred mountains and of your visit to the river.
You have given me life so that I may give away to the people.
I will be your brother forever.
Run under my belly.
I will take you right to the foot of the sacred mountains and you need not fear the spots.
Eagles cannot see you if you run under me.
All they will see is the back of buffalo.
I am of the prairie and I will fall on you if I try to go, but I am of the prairie and I will fall on you if I try to go up the mountains."
So little mouse ran under buffalo, secure and hidden from the spots, but with only one eye.
It was frightening.
The buffalo's great [unclear: "host"] shook the whole world every time he took a step, and finally they came to a place and buffalo stopped.*
*"This is where I must leave you, little brother," said buffalo.
"Thank you very much," said jumping mouse, "but you know, it's very frightening running under you with only one eye.
I was constantly in fear of your great earth-shaking [unclear: "hose"]."
"Your fear was for nothing," said buffalo, "for my way of walking is the sun dance away and I always know where my [unclear: "hose"] will fall.
I now must return to the prairie.
You will always find me there."*
*Jumping mouse and [unclear: "media"] began to investigate his new surroundings.
Even more things here than in the other places.
Busier things, new things, strange things, an abundance of seeds and other things mice like.
In his investigation of these things, suddenly he ran upon a gray wolf who was sitting there doing absolutely nothing.
"Hello brother, hello brother wolf," jumping mouse said.*
This is written all in the mail.
I don't know what the original was.
*The wolf's ears came alert and his eyes shone.
"Wolf, wolf, yes, that's what I am.
I am a wolf."
But then his mind dimmed again.
It was not long before he sat quietly again, completely without memory as to who he was.
Each time jumping mouse reminded him who he was, he became excited with the news, but then would soon forget.
"Such a great being," thought jumping mouse, "but he has no memory."
So jumping mouse went to the center of his new place and was quiet.
He listened for a long time to the beating of his heart, and suddenly he made up his mind.
He scurried back to where the wolf sat and he spoke.*
*"Brother wolf," jumping mouse said.
"Wolf, wolf," said the wolf.
"Yes, brother wolf," said jumping mouse.
"Please listen to me.
I know what will heal you.
It is one of my eyes, I think, and I want to give it to you.
You're a greater being than I.
I am only a mouse.
Please take it."
And jumping mouse stopped speaking.
His other eye flew out of his head and the wolf was made whole.
Tears fell down the cheeks of the wolf, but his little brother could not see them now, for he was blind.*
*"You are a great brother," said the wolf.
"For now I have my memory, but now you are blind.
I am the guide into the sacred mountains.
I will take you there.
There's a great medicine there.
The most beautiful lake in all the world, and in the world, all the world is reflected there.
The people, the lodges of the people and all the beings of the prairies and skies are there."
"Please take me there," jumping mouse said.
And wolf guided him through the pines to the medicine lake, and jumping mouse drank the water from the lake and the wolf described the beauty of it to him.*
*"I must leave you here," said wolf.
"I must return so I may guide others, and you can remain as long as you like."
"Thank you, my brother," said jumping mouse.
"But although I'm frightened to be alone, I know you must go so you can show others the way."
Jumping mouse sat there, trembling in fear.
It was no use running, for he was blind, but he knew an eagle would find him soon.
He felt a shadow on his back.
He heard the sound that eagles make.*
Maybe it's like our bald eagles.
*He braced himself for the shock, and the eagle hit and jumping mouse went to sleep.
Then he woke up.
The surprise of being alive was very great, but now he could see.
Everything was blurry, but the colors were beautiful.
"I can see, I can see," said jumping mouse again and and again.
A blurry shape came towards jumping mouse.
Jumping mouse squinted hard, but the shape remained a blur.
"Hello, brother," said the voice.
"Do you want some medicine?"
"Some medicine for me?" asked jumping mouse.
"Yes, yes.
Then crouched down as low as you can and jump as high as you can."*
*Jumping mouse did as he instructed.
He crouched as low as he could and jumped, and the wind caught him and carried him higher.
"Do not be afraid," the voice called him.
"Hang on to the wind and trust."
Jumping mouse did.
He closed his eyes and hung on to the wind and it carried him higher and higher.
Jumping mouse then opened his eyes and they were clear, and the higher he went, the clearer they became.
And jumping mouse saw his old friend upon a lily pad far below on the beautiful medicine lake.
It was frog.
"You have a new name again," said frog.
"You are eagle."*
That's the story of jumping mouse that Dogen reminded one of our members of on the hike, and it reminded me of something deep in my past.
I'm sure I heard it with very different [unclear: "years"] when I was 16, 17, but still there's plenty there.
So I'm curious to invite you to circle up.
Maybe this side and that side can make a circle of however many you are, five, and people online.
Is there anything in that story that mirrors your life or feels important or feels helpful?
It's sort of sweet and cute, but there's a lot there, things just on the outside of your consciousness, being drawn to find out, other people not understanding and believing you, right?
You need to keep going, making sacrifices, taking care of others and so on and so forth.
And in the end, we're all eagle.
Maybe we were all along.
Okay.
